messages.content: Write a comparison of two approaches to background jobs: a queue with workers, and scheduled batch runs. Around 200 words.

A queue with workers suits variable, high-frequency work. A producer pushes jobs onto a queue (SQS, Redis, RabbitMQ) and a pool of workers pulls them off as capacity allows. This gives near-real-time processing, natural retries via dead-letter queues, and horizontal scaling — add workers and throughput rises. The cost is operational complexity: you manage broker infrastructure, handle idempotency for retried jobs, and watch for backlog growth if workers fall behind producers.

Scheduled batch runs suit predictable, periodic work — nightly reports, data syncs, cleanup tasks. A cron trigger fires a job on a fixed interval, processes a bounded chunk of data, then exits. This is simpler to reason about: no broker, no long-running worker fleet, and failures are visible as a single run rather than scattered across a queue. The tradeoff is latency — work waits for the next scheduled slot — and batches can grow unwieldy if data volume spikes between runs.

In practice, teams often combine both: a queue handles user-triggered, latency-sensitive events, while batch jobs handle aggregate or maintenance work where a few minutes' delay is fine. If jobs are bursty and need fast turnaround, choose a queue. If work is inherently periodic and volume is predictable, a scheduled batch is simpler to build and cheaper to run.
